steps.text: You know trigonometry from school as triangle calculations. At university it becomes the study of periodic functions: oscillations, waves, Fourier series, complex numbers in polar form and rotation matrices all build on sine and cosine. For that you need the unit circle and radians.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Radians instead of degrees
2. Sine and cosine on the unit circle
3. Graphs, period, amplitude
4. Identities and addition theorems
5. Trigonometric equations and general triangles
steps.insight: The most important adjustment: at university radians almost always apply. \(\sin(1)\) means the sine of the angle \(1\) rad, not \(1°\).

steps.text: The radian measure measures an angle by the length of the corresponding arc on the unit circle (radius \(1\)). The full angle has circumference \(2\pi\).
steps.explanation:
\(\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{degrees} & 0° & 30° & 45° & 60° & 90° & 180° & 360° \\ \hline \text{radians} & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{4} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & 2\pi \end{array}\)

Example: \(135° = 135 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4}\). And \(\frac{5\pi}{6} \cdot \frac{180°}{\pi} = 150°\).

Why radians? Because then \(\sin x \approx x\) for small \(x\) and the derivative of the sine is simply \(\cos x\) – in degrees annoying factors would appear.
steps.insight: Remember: \(\pi\) rad \(= 180°\). Everything else follows by fraction arithmetic: \(\frac{\pi}{2} = 90°\), \(\frac{\pi}{3} = 60°\).

steps.text: On the unit circle (radius \(1\), centre at the origin), cosine and sine are the coordinates of the point at angle \(\varphi\):
steps.explanation:
The animation walks around the circle: at \(30°\), \(45°\), \(60°\), \(90°\) you read off the coordinates. The angle is always measured from the positive \(x\)-axis COUNTERCLOCKWISE.

The standard values:
\(\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \varphi & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{4} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \hline \sin\varphi & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 1 \\ \cos\varphi & 1 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \end{array}\)

Memory aid: sine at \(0, 30, 45, 60, 90\) is \(\frac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{4}}{2}\). Cosine runs backwards.
steps.insight: Because the point lies on the unit circle, always \(-1 \le \sin\varphi \le 1\) and \(-1 \le \cos\varphi \le 1\).

steps.text: From the symmetry of the circle follow the signs in the quadrants and many rules – without memorising.
steps.explanation:
Signs: in the \(1\)st quadrant \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) are positive, in the \(2\)nd only \(\sin\), in the \(3\)rd only \(\tan\), in the \(4\)th only \(\cos\).

Examples without a calculator:
• \(\sin 150° = \sin(180° - 30°) = \sin 30° = \frac{1}{2}\)
• \(\cos 120° = -\cos 60° = -\frac{1}{2}\)
• \(\sin 210° = -\sin 30° = -\frac{1}{2}\)

After a full circle (\(2\pi\)) everything repeats: sine and cosine are \(2\pi\)-periodic, tangent is \(\pi\)-periodic.
steps.insight: Reduce to a reference angle between \(0\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), then determine the sign from the quadrant.

steps.text: In a right triangle the definitions agree with the unit circle:
steps.explanation:
Example: a \(5\,\text{m}\) ladder leans against a wall at an angle of \(60°\). How high does it reach? Height \(= 5 \sin 60° = 5 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 4.33\,\text{m}\); distance from the wall \(5 \cos 60° = 2.5\,\text{m}\).

In a triangle only acute angles are possible. The unit circle extends sine and cosine to all angles – including negative ones and those above \(360°\).
steps.insight: Set your calculator to RAD or DEG! The most common mistake with angles is the wrong mode.

steps.text: If you plot the sine of the angle against the angle, the sine curve appears. The animation "unwraps" the circle: the height of the revolving point is the function value.
steps.explanation:
The cosine is the sine curve shifted \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) to the left. Both are bounded and periodic.

General sine function:
\(f(x) = A \sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D\)
• \(|A|\): amplitude (height of the oscillation)
• \(\frac{2\pi}{|B|}\): period
• \(C\): phase shift to the right
• \(D\): midline (shift upwards)

Example: \(3\sin(2x)\) has amplitude \(3\) and period \(\pi\). \(\cos x + 1\) oscillates between \(0\) and \(2\) about the midline \(y = 1\).
steps.section: Chapter 3 · Graphs of sine, cosine, tangent
steps.insight: A larger \(B\) means faster oscillation: more periods fit in the same stretch.

steps.text: The tangent is the quotient \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) – and the slope of the line from the origin to the circle point.
steps.explanation:
At the places where \(\cos x = 0\) (\(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \ldots\)), the tangent is undefined: there are vertical asymptotes (poles).

The range is all of \(\mathbb{R}\). The tangent is odd (\(\tan(-x) = -\tan x\)) and strictly increasing between two poles.

Known values: \(\tan 45° = 1\), \(\tan 30° = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\), \(\tan 60° = \sqrt{3}\). At \(90°\) the value would be infinite – undefined.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · Graphs of sine, cosine, tangent
steps.insight: \(\tan\varphi\) is the slope of a line with inclination angle \(\varphi\): \(m = \tan\varphi\).

steps.text: The most important identity follows from the Pythagorean theorem on the unit circle: the point \((\cos x, \sin x)\) has distance \(1\) from the origin.
steps.explanation:
With it one value determines the other – up to the sign. Example: \(\sin x = \frac{3}{5}\).
• \(\cos^2 x = 1 - \frac{9}{25} = \frac{16}{25}\), so \(\cos x = \pm\frac{4}{5}\).
• If \(x\) lies in the \(1\)st quadrant: \(\cos x = +\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\tan x = \frac{3}{4}\).
• If \(x\) lies in the \(2\)nd quadrant: \(\cos x = -\frac{4}{5}\).

Note the notation \(\sin^2 x = (\sin x)^2\), not \(\sin(x^2)\).
steps.insight: Given \(\sin x\) and the quadrant, \(x\) is completely determined. The sign comes from the quadrant.

steps.text: The addition theorems compute sine and cosine of a sum from the values of the individual angles:
steps.explanation:
The double-angle formulas follow with \(a = b = x\). The three forms of \(\cos 2x\) come from \(\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1\).

Application: exact value of \(\sin 75°\):
\(\sin(45° + 30°) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4} \approx 0.9659\).

From \(\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x\) we get \(\sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\) – you need this rewriting when integrating \(\sin^2 x\).
steps.insight: Typical mistake: \(\sin(a + b) = \sin a + \sin b\). That is wrong: \(\sin 90° = 1\), but \(\sin 45° + \sin 45° = \sqrt{2}\).

steps.text: Trigonometric equations have infinitely many solutions because of periodicity – or you restrict to an interval such as \([0, 2\pi]\).
steps.explanation:
Procedure:
1. Find the principal value with the inverse function: \(\arcsin \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
2. Second solution by symmetry: \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\), so \(\pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\).
3. Add the period.

Further cases:
• \(\cos x = c\): solutions \(\pm\arccos c + 2k\pi\).
• \(\tan x = c\): \(x = \arctan c + k\pi\) (only one solution per period).
• \(\cos x = 0\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi\).

The inverse functions: \(\arcsin \in [-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]\), \(\arccos \in [0, \pi]\), \(\arctan \in (-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2})\). They only give the principal value.
steps.insight: Calculators and \(\arcsin\) always give only ONE solution. You find the second by symmetry on the unit circle.

steps.text: For arbitrary triangles (without a right angle) you need two laws:
steps.explanation:
• Law of sines: the ratio of a side to the sine of the opposite angle is constant. Useful when a side-angle pair is known.
• Law of cosines: generalised Pythagoras. For \(\gamma = 90°\), \(\cos\gamma = 0\) and \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\) remains.

Example law of cosines: \(a = 5\), \(b = 7\), \(\gamma = 60°\): \(c^2 = 25 + 49 - 70 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 39\), so \(c \approx 6.24\).

Example law of sines: \(a = 10\), \(\alpha = 45°\), \(\beta = 60°\): \(b = \frac{a \sin\beta}{\sin\alpha} = 10 \cdot \frac{0.866}{0.7071} \approx 12.25\).
steps.insight: Law of cosines: two sides and the included angle (or three sides). Law of sines: a side and its opposite angle known.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Radians: \(\pi\) rad \(= 180°\). All standard angles as fractions of \(\pi\).

2. Unit circle: \((\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\). Exact values at \(0, \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\); symmetries give the rest.

3. Sine and cosine: period \(2\pi\), amplitude \(|A|\), period \(\frac{2\pi}{|B|}\). Tangent: period \(\pi\), poles at \(\frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi\).

4. \(\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1\). Addition theorems and double angles.

5. Equations: principal value plus symmetry plus period. Law of sines and cosines in a general triangle.
steps.insight: Congratulations! Sine and cosine return in "Complex Numbers" (polar form), "Differential Calculus" (derivatives) and "Linear Mappings" (rotation matrices).
